reasoning: Extensive scientific research, including rigorous double-blind placebo-controlled trials, has repeatedly failed to establish a causal link between dietary MSG consumption and symptoms such as headaches, numbness, or "Chinese restaurant syndrome." The term originated from an anecdotal 1968 letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine, which sparked widespread public panic and xenophobic stigma rather than scientifically validated findings. Major food safety and health authorities worldwide, including the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO), classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS), noting that the human body metabolizes added MSG identically to the naturally occurring glutamates found in foods like tomatoes and aged cheese. Placebo-controlled studies show that reported symptoms occur at similar rates between MSG and placebo groups.
title: MSG causes headaches — 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'
